prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it with more confidence than many of them currently do, because the case against it rests on a picture of the classroom that is already out of date and on a picture of the future that is more certain than the evidence allows. The argument for dropping it is easy to state and sounds modern: children will type for most of their adult lives, the hours spent on looped ascenders could go to reading or coding, and print letters are perfectly legible anyway. Each of those points contains something true, and I will come back to them, but none of them survives contact with what a child is actually doing when she learns to write by hand, or with what a school day demands of a nine-year-old holding a pencil.

Begin with the plain fact that most schoolwork is still handwritten, and so is every public examination in England and in most other countries, which means that a child's handwriting is the channel through which nearly everything she knows has to pass for at least the next decade of her education. A pupil who prints each letter separately lifts her pen after every stroke, repositions it, and starts again, so that a single page of writing contains thousands of small interruptions that a joined hand removes. The evidence on raw speed is mixed, and there are quick, neat printers who outpace sloppy joiners, but the pupils who struggle most are usually the ones whose printing is slow and effortful, and joining offers them a route to a continuous movement that their separate letters never allow. The speed matters less for its own sake than for what it frees, since a child who must think about forming each letter has less attention left for what she wants to say, how the word is spelled, and where the sentence is heading. Virginia Berninger and her colleagues have shown across many studies that children whose letter production is automatic write longer and better compositions than children whose letter production is still costing them effort, and the practical implication for a teacher is that handwriting has to be taught until it becomes automatic rather than left to arrive on its own.

Joined-up writing is the natural way to reach that automaticity, because it turns letters into movements that belong to words. When a child learns to write "ing" or "the" as a single flowing gesture, the hand begins to store spelling patterns as motor sequences, and teachers of spelling have long observed that children who struggle to recall a word on paper will often find it again by writing it out in joined script and letting the hand lead. The research here is thinner than enthusiasts claim, and anyone who says science has proved cursive improves spelling is overreaching, but the underlying logic is sound and fits the broader finding that handwriting differs from typing in ways that matter to learning. Karin James's imaging studies with pre-literate children found that practising letters by hand, but not by typing or tracing, activated the reading circuits of the brain, and Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer found that students taking notes by hand retained concepts better than those typing, in part because handwriting forces compression and choice. Neither study is about cursive as such, yet both point the same way: the slow, embodied act of making marks does cognitive work that pressing keys does not, and a school that abandons the most developed form of that act is giving up something it has not yet found a replacement for.

The strongest case for joining comes from the children who find writing hardest. Occupational therapists and specialists in dyslexia and dyspraxia have for decades recommended a continuous, joined style for pupils who reverse letters, because a joined hand makes it harder to confuse b and d, which in print are the same shape facing different ways but in cursive begin and end in different places, and because the rhythm of a joined word gives a child with poor sequencing a built-in guide to the order of its letters. Some of these claims rest on clinical experience more than on controlled trials, and I would not rest the whole argument on them, but when a method is cheap, harmless to the other children, and favoured by the people who work daily with those who struggle, the burden of proof falls on the people proposing to remove it. A school that teaches joined writing to everyone also avoids the quiet unfairness of teaching it only to those whose parents know to ask, and it avoids singling out the dyslexic child as the one who has to learn a different system from her classmates.

The best objection is that typing is the skill of the future, and the objection is a good one, but it proves less than it seems to. Typing can be taught alongside handwriting, and the two do not compete for the same scarce resource in any way that a sensible timetable cannot manage: a child needs perhaps ten or fifteen minutes of handwriting practice a day in the early years, and that investment, which tapers off as fluency arrives, buys a skill that will serve her for life. The experience of countries that went the other way is instructive. Finland made cursive optional in its 2016 national curriculum and emphasised keyboard skills, and the decision attracted worldwide attention as a sign of where education was heading, yet the debate has not gone quietly in the years since, and in the United States, where Common Core left cursive out, a majority of states have since passed laws bringing it back, partly in response to teachers who reported that pupils could not sign their names or read a handwritten note from a grandparent. A reform that has to be walked back in so many places was perhaps not as obviously progressive as it looked on the day it was announced.

There is also a claim about what the school owes the child, which concerns the written record of the culture she is growing up in. Letters, diaries, marginal notes in library books, the recipe card in a relative's drawer and the front of a historical document are overwhelmingly written in joined script, and a child who cannot read cursive is cut off from them in a way that a short course of instruction would have prevented. Reading joined writing is easier than producing it, and one could imagine teaching recognition alone, but recognition without production tends to be shallow, since the shapes of unfamiliar letterforms are learned most securely by making them, and a pupil who has never written a cursive capital G will puzzle over it long after a pupil who has. The same goes for the signature, which remains the way adults authenticate agreements on paper and which is far more naturally a joined than a printed gesture. None of this is sentimental: it is about whether children can take part in everyday adult life, in which pen and paper have turned out to be more durable than many forecasters expected.

What teaching joined-up handwriting well requires is also worth saying, because much of the case against it is really a case against bad teaching. Schools that begin cursive late, in year three or four, after children have built habits of print, force them to unlearn and relearn, which is the worst of both worlds and produces the sullen, half-joined scrawl that gives the method its poor reputation. The better approach, used in many schools that report good results, is to teach letters with the exit strokes from the beginning, so that the child never learns a separate print alphabet she will later have to abandon, and to introduce joins gradually once the letter shapes are secure, with short, frequent, supervised practice rather than long copying exercises. It also means accepting that children will arrive at their own personal hands in adolescence, as every adult has, and that the goal of the primary years is a sound foundation to adapt from, rather than uniformity of slope or the loops of a copperplate nobody has used for a century. Teachers who work this way tend to find that the children who dreaded writing become less reluctant once the physical effort of it falls, and that is an outcome worth far more than an elegant page.

I do not claim that joined writing is a magic ingredient, and anyone who tells you that it raises test scores or builds character is selling something the research does not support. My claim is narrower and, I think, harder to dislodge: handwriting remains the dominant means by which children show what they know, fluent handwriting frees mental effort for thinking and composing, a joined style is the most efficient way to achieve fluency for most children and an especially good one for those who struggle, and the costs of teaching it are small when the teaching is done early and done well. Against that stands a prediction that handwriting will vanish, which has been made confidently for thirty years and has not yet come true, and a reasonable policy does not bet a generation's basic skills on a forecast that keeps slipping. If keyboards one day do make the pen obsolete in schools, the children who learned both will have lost nothing, whereas the children who learned only one will have lost a good deal if the forecast turns out wrong. For that reason, and for the sake of the pupils who will find the pen their hardest tool and need it to be as easy to use as it can be, primary schools should go on teaching joined-up handwriting.
